idea: A huge '#' with the old libra-pondo abbreviation '℔' (an 'lb' with a stroke through it) drawn faintly behind it, captioned 'octothorpe (n.): named at Bell Labs in the 1960s. Probably descended from ℔, a pound of something.' Everyone types the mark daily, but few know its odd official name or its likely origin in the scales of commerce.

A large '@' drawn in a Renaissance merchant's cursive, with the line 'Florence, 4 May 1536: one @ of wine.' The earliest known dated use of the sign is in a letter by the merchant Francesco Lapi, where it stands for an amphora, a measure of wine. The email symbol turns out to be a wine jar.

The word 'Ye' set in blackletter, with the Y redrawn as the old letter thorn 'þ' beside it, captioned 'Pronounced "the". It was always "the".' Early English printers used continental type that had no þ, so they swapped in a look-alike y. It debunks every 'Ye Olde' sign in one elegant glyph.

A newspaper column clipping reset in 19th-century type with one phrase picked out: 'o.k. — all correct', captioned 'Boston Morning Post, 23 March 1839. Misspelled on purpose.' The world's most-used word started as a joke abbreviation in a fad for comic misspellings. It's for people who like big things with silly origins.

A single tall Arabic alif with a column of diamond-shaped pen dots stacked beside it like a ruler, captioned 'Ibn Muqla, 10th century: every letter measured in dots of the pen.' The Abbasid vizier is credited with proportioned script, where each letter's size is set by rhombic dots from the reed pen. It's calligraphy as geometry, and a natural partner for the golden-angle seed head.

The Chinese character 永 ('eternity') drawn with brush strokes, each of its eight strokes numbered 1 to 8, captioned 'Eight Principles of Yong: one word holds every stroke.' Calligraphy students have long practised this one character because it contains all eight basic stroke types. It's beautiful and a whole curriculum in a single sign.

The Cherokee syllabary laid out as a clean specimen grid of its signs, captioned 'Sequoyah, 1821. He could not read any language, so he invented a way to write his own.' Within a few years, much of the Cherokee Nation could read. It's about how one determined person turned an idea into literacy for a whole people.

Several lines of Greek capitals that run left to right, then right to left with the letters mirrored, then back, captioned 'boustrophedon: "as the ox turns" while ploughing.' Early Greek inscriptions really were written this way, like a plough going up and down a field. It's a striking pattern that makes the wearer's chest a field of letters.

A short specimen line in Caslon with the heading 'BASKERVILLE' over it, captioned 'Franklin's prank, 1760: a critic said this Baskerville hurt his eyes. It was Caslon.' Benjamin Franklin tore the title off a Caslon specimen to test a man who complained about Baskerville, and wrote to Baskerville about it. It's a sly shirt about how much of taste is the label.

A dictionary entry set in 1930s style: 'dord (n.) Physics & Chem. Density.', captioned 'A word that never existed. Webster's, 1934–1947.' The ghost word came from a slip reading 'D or d' (abbreviations for density) that was misfiled as a word; it was spotted in 1939 and removed in 1947. It's for editors, and for anyone who has trusted a reference book too much.

The word 'serendipity' set like a fine book title, with 'Horace Walpole, letter of 28 January 1754' below and a small line: 'from The Three Princes of Serendip, who kept finding things they weren't looking for.' Walpole coined the word in a letter, after a Persian fairy tale. It's a lucky word with a known birthday.

The word 'Fraktur' in a dense, beautiful blackletter, with a typed date beneath: '3 January 1941.' and the line 'The day the Nazis banned the typeface they had called German.' Martin Bormann's circular suddenly declared Fraktur to be 'Schwabacher Jewish letters' and ordered a switch to roman type. It's a quiet, sharp point that typefaces get politics forced on them.

A line of the N'Ko alphabet, running right to left, captioned 'N'Ko, 1949. Solomana Kanté's answer to the claim that African languages could not be written.' Kanté designed the script for the Manding languages, and its name means 'I say' in all of them. It's elegant letterforms with a point of view built in.

Four triangles in a row, ᐯ ᐱ ᐳ ᐸ, labelled 'pe pi po pa', captioned 'Cree syllabics, 1840: turn the consonant to change the vowel.' In James Evans's script one shape rotates to show which vowel follows, so the system can be learned in days. It's a clever writing system that looks like minimal geometric art.

A single vertical word in traditional Mongolian script running down the shirt, with the note 'Top to bottom, columns left to right. Borrowed from the Uyghurs under Genghis Khan.' The script was adopted in the early 13th century and is still official in Inner Mongolia. It's a tall, flowing letterform most people have never seen.

The Chinese character 休 ('rest') drawn large, with its two parts pulled slightly apart and labelled 亻 'person' and 木 'tree', captioned 'To rest: a person leaning on a tree.' It's a true and gentle etymology in one sign, and it fits right next to the botanical prints.

A ladder of the same word set in rising sizes, each labelled with its old printer's name: Diamond, Pearl, Agate, Nonpareil, Minion, Brevier, Bourgeois, Long Primer, Small Pica, Pica, English, Great Primer. Captioned 'Before points, type sizes had names.' These were real working names in British and American foundries, and they read like a poem.

The Spanish word 'año' set large, with the tilde drawn as a tiny squashed letter n, and the caption 'ñ was nn. The tilde is a little n written on top.' Medieval scribes saved space by writing a doubled n as one n with a small n above, as in Latin annus becoming año. It's a smart reveal about a mark people see every day.

A Phoenician harbour drawn in fine line beside the word BIBLE, with a chain of words: 'Byblos → byblos (papyrus) → biblion (book) → Bible.' The Greeks named papyrus after the port of Byblos, which traded it, and their word for 'book' came from that. The holiest book in the West is named after a paper market.

The word 'robot' set in a crisp grotesque, followed by its entry: 'from Czech robota, "forced labour". Coined by Josef Čapek for his brother Karel's play R.U.R., 1920.' The word was born in a play about manufactured workers who rebel. It's a timely shirt that reminds you what the word originally meant.
